> I'm trying to implement a spatial non-stationary model using a binomial response. I'm aware that the selection of hyperparameters values is crucial in this kind of model, and the ones I'm using (corresponding to the original paper) are not proper for the selected data, but I'm also sure that there are other silly mistakes. I will appreciate it if you can point these out for me in order to achieve the estimation. I will also appreciate any recommendations for the selection of hyperparameter values, considering that the original priors are very informative. The following code corresponds to the model fitting step, but I'm attaching the complete code with the necessary data in order to reproduce the example. Thank you in advance for your help an guidance.
>

> formula.ns = y ~ -1 +
>   f(intercept,
>     model = "linear",

Every time I try to run my code, I get an error that INLA has crashed.

My code is :

rprior <- list(theta = list(prior = "pccor1", param = c(0, 0.9)))

formula <- y ~ 0 + b0 + f(s,
                          model = spde, group = s.group,
                          control.group = list(model = "ar1", hyper = rprior)
)

res <- inla(formula,
            data = inla.stack.data(stk.full),
            control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE,
                                     A = inla.stack.A(stk.full)),
            verbose = TRUE)

The error is get is :

Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed() : The inla-program exited with an error. Unless you interupted it yourself, please rerun with verbose=TRUE and check the output carefully. If this does not help, please contact the developers at <he...@r-inla.org>. Error in inla.core.safe(formula = formula, family = family, contrasts = contrasts, : *** Fail to get good enough initial values. Maybe it is due to something else.

data("DT_halfdiallel")

 DT$malef<-as.factor(DT$male)

####model using overlay
modh<-mmec(sugar~1, random=~vsc(isc(overlay(femalef,malef))) +genof,nIters=3, data=DT,verbose=FALSE)
summary(modh)$varcomp

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I want to model a non-linear relationship using  a random walk model. Below is my approach:

# simulate data
N = 100 # num of observations
x = sort(runif(N, -1 , 1)) # sort for line plot
eps = rnorm(N,0,.1)
fx = x^2 - x^3 + 2*x
y = fx + eps

df = data.frame(x=x, y=y)

# binning the predictor
df$x_binned = inla.group(df$x, n = 20, method = "cut")

# model definition
formula = y ~ f(x_binned, model = 'rw1')

# fitting the model
model = inla(formula, data = df, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))

# extracting the estimated effects
bin_id = model$summary.random$x_binned$ID
bin_mean = model$summary.random$x_binned$mean
post_pred = model$summary.fitted.values$mean

plot(x,y)
lines(bin_id, mean, col = 'red')
lines(x, post_pred, col = 'blue')

which results in the below plot:

Does anyone know why the red line posterior mean of the bins is systematically underestimating the true values? What explains the gap between the two lines?

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

If you look at summary(model) I expect you’ll see that it added an intercept parameter to the model. That’s a feature of the R formula methods. I recommend explicitly controlling whether there should be an intercept or not:
Automatic intercept:
y ~ f(…)
Explicit intercept:
y ~ 1 + f(…)
No intercept:
y ~ 0 + f(…)   or   y ~ -1 + f(…)

Finn

messages.subject_clean: inla.read.graph issue
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am working with data in a secure environment and unfortunately cannot share any files. My code (similar example below) runs fine until I attempt to load the adjacency matrix (the bolded line). When I try to run that I get the following error:

Error in if (s[k] + offset == 0L) { :
                  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

Any insight on what is going on here would be very helpful. Thank you!

Beth

Code:
#import shapefile
shapefile.gen <- readShapePoly("./LSOA11_London.shp")

#create adjacency matrix
temp <- poly2nb(shapefile.gen )
nb2INLA("London.graph", temp)
LDN.adj <- paste(getwd(),"/LDN.graph",sep="")

#load LSOA adjacency matrix
London.adj <- inla.read.graph(filename=" LDN.adj")
image(inla.graph2matrix(London.adj),xlab="",ylab="")

model<-inla(formula = formula,data = mydata,
             family = "zeroinflatedpoisson0", E = E,verbose = T,
             control.compute = list(dic=T,cpo=T,waic=T),

messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure about the time1 NAs, but for Var1 and Var2, the NAs are introduced by the inla.stack() construction.  You're much better off doing the conversion to dummy (0/1) variables yourself first, since that would give you complete control over how the factor variables are interpreted. E.g. first calling "MyVars = model.matrix(~ 1 + Var1 + Var2, data = ...)", and then using "... ~ 0 + MyVars" instead of "... ~ Var1 + Var2" in the inla formula, and as (matrix) input to inla.stack would probably give you what you want.

Finn

A sexta-feira, 11 de agosto de 2023 à(s) 10:51:43 UTC+1, Finn Lindgren escreveu:
> I'm not sure about the time1 NAs, but for Var1 and Var2, the NAs are introduced by the inla.stack() construction.  You're much better off doing the conversion to dummy (0/1) variables yourself first, since that would give you complete control over how the factor variables are interpreted. E.g. first calling "MyVars = model.matrix(~ 1 + Var1 + Var2, data = ...)", and then using "... ~ 0 + MyVars" instead of "... ~ Var1 + Var2" in the inla formula, and as (matrix) input to inla.stack would probably give you what you want.
>
> Finn

> > I'm not sure about the time1 NAs, but for Var1 and Var2, the NAs are introduced by the inla.stack() construction.  You're much better off doing the conversion to dummy (0/1) variables yourself first, since that would give you complete control over how the factor variables are interpreted. E.g. first calling "MyVars = model.matrix(~ 1 + Var1 + Var2, data = ...)", and then using "... ~ 0 + MyVars" instead of "... ~ Var1 + Var2" in the inla formula, and as (matrix) input to inla.stack would probably give you what you want.

> > > I'm not sure about the time1 NAs, but for Var1 and Var2, the NAs are introduced by the inla.stack() construction.  You're much better off doing the conversion to dummy (0/1) variables yourself first, since that would give you complete control over how the factor variables are interpreted. E.g. first calling "MyVars = model.matrix(~ 1 + Var1 + Var2, data = ...)", and then using "... ~ 0 + MyVars" instead of "... ~ Var1 + Var2" in the inla formula, and as (matrix) input to inla.stack would probably give you what you want.

messages.subject_clean: Backwards selection for LGCP model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am fitting a model with 5 covariates included in the "full model." I am trying to use backwards selection to get to the "best" model (assuming that this should be measured through DIC). The code I've got for the full model is as below:

cmpfull <- coordinates ~
  LRoad(Covariates$LRoad, model = "linear") +
  Forest(Covariates$Forest, model = "linear") +
  SRoad(Covariates$SRoad, model = "linear") +
  Village(Covariates$Village, model = "linear") +
  mySPDE(coordinates, model = matern) +
  lsig(1) +
  Intercept(1)

hn <- function(distance, lsig) {1 - exp(-(distance / (exp(lsig)))^-1)}

form <- coordinates + distance ~ mySPDE +
  log(hn(distance, lsig)) +
  Intercept + log(2)

matern <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh,
                              prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01),
                              prior.range = c(10, 0.9))

fitfull <- lgcp(
  components = cmpfull,
  data = nests,
  samplers = transects,
  domain = list(
    coordinates = mesh,
    distance = INLA::inla.mesh.1d(seq(0, W, length.out = 30))
  ),
  formula = form,
  options = list(bru_initial = list(lsig = 2),
                 bru_verbose=4)
)

What would be the correct way to use backwards selection to get to a model that only includes the most powerful covariates? Is there a way to do this without going through every iteration of the model to see which has the lowest DIC? Any help much appreciated!

messages.body_plain:
Hi Lucy,

disregarding the wider question of whether these types of variable
selection methods should really be used at all, then no, there isn't
really a faster way than going through all the models that the
backwards selection method needs to compare.
You can/should help it by setting initial values though, so the
optimiser gets some help; As long as it's only the covariates, it's
easy; just supply values for the latent variable estimate for each
component in bru_initial.
Something like
  bru_linitial=list(LRoad = other_model_result$summary.fixed["LRoad",
"mode"], ...)

Finn

messages.body_plain:
It seems your data uses metres as units, but your max.edge value seems to be intended to be in km? It might be that it’s trying to create a very very dense mesh.

Make sure to install the very latest version of fmesher, and replace the inla.mesh.2d call with a call to the fmesher function fm_mesh_2d (same parameters) and let me know if that helps or not (after making sure max.edge is in the appropriate units).
When converting the INLA package version of fmesher to a standalone package, I fixed some potential infinite loops that could happen for some special input data, so the new function should be more robust.  We haven’t merged the branch of INLA that will use the new fmesher package yet (but expect to do so soon, once fmesher gets onto CRAN).  I’m currently doing the last bug fixes and documentation of fmesher, and will send it to CRAN in the coming days most likely.

Finn

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Failure of spatio-temporal modeling based on binomial
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I am fitting a spatio-temporal additive model with covariates using negative binomial likelihood to a large count data (n>36000 records). The code works fine without any issue in R version 4.31., R-INLA 23.08.08 under windows 10 x64.
# ###### formula and INLA commands used ######:
lcar.iid.ad <http://lcar.iid.ad> <- O ~ f(ID.area, model="generic1", Cmatrix=Q_Leroux, constr=TRUE,         hyper=list(prec=list(prior=sdunif),beta=list(prior=lunif))) +
            f(ID.month, model="iid", constr=TRUE, hyper=list(theta=list(prior="loggamma",param=c(1,0.01)))) + X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5 + X6 + X7 + X8

model_lcar.iid.ad <http://model_lcar.iid.ad><-INLA::inla(lcar.iid.ad <http://lcar.iid.ad>, family="nbinomial", data=Data.INLA, E=E, control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE, link=1,cdf=c(log(1))), control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, waic=TRUE), control.inla=list(strategy="simplified.laplace", npoints=21),verbose=TRUE)

Recently, I have switched over to a new laptop MacPro M2 and tried running the same code using R version 4.3.1 (2023-06-16), under: macOS Ventura 13.4.1, and R-INLA version 23.08.08. After several function evaluations, it crashed with the following error:

Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed() :
  The inla-program exited with an error. Unless you interupted it yourself, please rerun with verbose=TRUE and check the output carefully.
  If this does not help, please contact the developers at <he...@r-inla.org>.
Error in inla.core.safe(formula = formula, family = family, contrasts = contrasts,  :
  *** Failed to get good enough initial values. Maybe it is due to something else.

 I would request you all to kindly help me in resolving this issue.

Thanks in advance
S. Subramanian

Dear INLA users,

I am trying to implement the following two likelihoods model in INLA:

x = Intercept_x + Slope_x * time + error
y = Intercept_y + Slope_y * time + beta*(Intercept_x + Slope_x*time) + error

where the linear predictor of x is copied in the linear predictor of y, scaling the effects with a new parameter beta estimated by INLA from the data.

I wrote the following code to do so:

fixed.effects <- list(Intercept_y = c(rep(NA, N_obs), rep(1, N_obs)),
                        t_y = c(rep(NA, N_obs), data$t),

                        t = c(data$t, data$t))

random.effects <- list(Intercept_x = c(rep(1, N_obs), rep(NA, N_obs)),
                          t_x = c(rep(1, N_obs), rep(NA, N_obs)),

                          Intercept_x_scaled = c(rep(NA, N_obs), rep(1, N_obs)),
                          t_x_scaled = c(rep(NA, N_obs), rep(1, N_obs)))

INLA_data <- c(fixed.effects, random.effects)
INLA_data$Y <- list(c(data$x, rep(NA, N_obs)),
                      c(rep(NA, N_obs), data$y))

INLA_formula = Y ~ -1 +
    # fixed effects of x
    f(Intercept_x) + f(t_x, t) +
    # scaled fixed effects of x
    f(Intercept_x_scaled, copy = "Intercept_x", hyper = list(beta = list(fixed=FALSE))) +
    f(t_x_scaled, t, copy = "t_x", same.as <http://same.as> = 'Intercept_x_scaled', hyper = list(beta = list(fixed=FALSE))) +
    # fixed effects of y
    Intercept_y + t_y

M2 <- inla(INLA_formula, family = c("gaussian","gaussian"), data = INLA_data)

I think that the structure of the code is correct, but looking at the results more in detail it seems to me that the copy feature is not really working in the Intercept.
Here below you can see the results of the Intercept_x and Slope_x scaled and not.

> M2$summary.hyperpar  mean Precision for the Gaussian observations 0.30163126 Precision for the Gaussian observations[2] 0.01130564 Precision for Intercept_x 0.03346231 Precision for t_x 104.90106577 Beta for Intercept_x_scaled 1.05396431
> M2$summary.random$Intercept_x  ID mean 1 1 10.20079 > M2$summary.random$Intercept_x_scaled  ID mean
1 1 1.799346

> M2$summary.random$t_x  ID mean 1 1 -0.163891 > M2$summary.random$t_x_scaled  ID mean 1 1 -0.176995

As you can see, the posterior mean of the beta parameter is 1.0539. Thus, following the definition given in Section 6.5.1 in the "Bayesian inference with INLA" book, the estimates of the slopes t_x are almost identical, with a little difference given by the tiny added noise. The scaled intercept, instead, is not equal to beta*intercept_x + noise.

Do you know what could be the problem? Changing the prior or working with the initial values does not seem to work.

Thanks in advance,
Chiara

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I came across with the question for the second-type model you guys discussed.

Now I have multiple likelihood (2 outcomes), as well as multiple level (longitudinal data with just random intercepts),
I want to estimate the correlation between random intercepts from two separated likelihoods.

So I used "iid2d", but it seems it does not work for the way I want.
(BTW, it seems work if I have two correlated random slopes no random intercept).

$$
\begin{split}
& \begin{cases}
x_{ij} \ | \ b_{1i} = \beta_{X0} + \beta_{X1}  \times {gender}_{x_i} + \beta_{X2} \times visit_{x_{ij}}  + \beta_{X_3} \times group_i +
b_{1i} + \epsilon_{x_{ij}}  \\
y_{ij} \ |  b_{2i} = \beta_{Y0} + \beta_{Y1}  \times {gender}_{yi} + \beta_{Y2} \times visit_{y_{ij}} + \beta_{Y_3} \times group_i +
 b_{2i} +  \epsilon_{y_{ij}} \\
\end{cases} \\
& \begin{bmatrix}
  b_1\\b_2
\end{bmatrix} \sim
MVN
\begin{pmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix}
    0\\0
  \end{bmatrix} ,
  \begin{pmatrix}
    \sigma_{b_1}^2 & \rho\sigma_{b_1}\sigma_{b_2}\\
    \rho\sigma_{b_1}\sigma_{b_2} & \sigma_{b_2}^2
  \end{pmatrix}
\end{pmatrix} \\
&\epsilon_{x_{ij}} \sim N(0, \sigma_{\epsilon_X}^2)\\
&\epsilon_{y_{ij}} \sim N(0, \sigma_{\epsilon_Y}^2)
\end{split}
$$

I am doing a 100 dataset simulation. So far INLA works perfect for fixed effects, $sigma_{b1}$, and error terms $\epsilons$,
however I do not understand what is going on with the correlation $\rho$ and the $sigma_{b2}$.
I assume INLA does not parametrize the model as I expected.

Most of the examples I saw are correlated random slope and random intercept.
But I want to model two correlated random intercepts from two likelihood.
Any idea?

Thanks!

Randy

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Currently I am using "iid2d" either with scaled or no scaled random intercept

sim.joint1 <- y ~  -1 + I + gender + visit + group +
    f(idxy,
       model = "iid2d",
       n = 2 * n,
      hyper = list(theta1 = list(param = c(4, 0.001, 0.001, 0))))

sim.joint2 <- y ~  -1 + I + gender + visit + group +
    f(idx,
       model = "iid2d",
       n = 2 * n,
      hyper = list(theta1 = list(param = c(4, 0.001, 0.001, 0)))) +
    f(idy, copy = "idx",
        fixed = FALSE)

 inla.joint1 <- try(inla(sim.joint1,
                     family = c("gaussian", "gaussian"),
                     # control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
                     # control.compute = list(dic = TRUE),
                     data = data71))

This model should be straight forward, and its weird you do not get the
correlation and sigma_{b2} correct. There is no confounding going on,
right, like with with noise variances?  You still get it wrong if you
fix the likelihoods to be Gaussians with known precisions?

I guess you do simulations so you can chose i=1..I, and j=1..J, and its
still bad even with large I and J ?

The 'iid2d' model use directly the (transformed) correlation as the
hyperparameter, hence you should get it directly out in the results.

Can you retry the same model without all covariates, ie just the iid2d
model?  This is also one of the examples in inla.doc('iid2d')

There is a recent implementation, 'iidkd' that scales better for higher
'k', which uses a different parameterisation, but this should not change
anything for dimension 2.

Best
H

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dr. Rue,

I assume probably INLA parametrized in different way.

Here is the result and the code for 200 individuals each with 5 time repeated measures.
INLA worked perfectly well for the fixed estimates and residuals.

```
inla_sim <- function(seed,
                     nid = 200, # num of individuals
                     eachid = 5, # visit num for each individual
                     sigma_bx, # random effect for the first outcome
                     lambda, # scaled up for hte second outcome
                     rho, # correlation between the two outcomes
                     sigma_ex = 1, # residual for the first outcome
                     sigma_ey = 0.5, # residual for the second outcome
                     ## add intercepts
                     InterceptX,
                     InterceptY){
  set.seed(seed)

  n = eachid * nid
  id <- rep(1:200, each = 5)
  # browser()
  ## sigma_y is a scaled sigma_x
  sigma_by <- lambda * sigma_bx
  Sigma <- matrix(data = c(sigma_bx^2, rho * sigma_bx * sigma_by,
                           rho * sigma_bx * sigma_by, sigma_by^2),
                  nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
  errorX <- rnorm(n, 0, sigma_ex)
  errorY <- rnorm(n, 0, sigma_ey)

  randomXY <- MASS::mvrnorm(n = nid,
                            mu = c(0, 0),
                            Sigma = Sigma) %>%
    as.data.frame()

  ## the outcomes in two different cols
  y <- matrix(NA, nrow = 2 * n, ncol = 2)
  y[1:n, 1] <- InterceptX + randomXY[id, 1] + errorX
  y[n + 1:n, 2] <- InterceptY  + randomXY[id, 2] + errorY

  ## indicator intercept cols
  I <- matrix(NA, nrow = 2 * n, ncol = 2)
  I[1:n, 1] <- 1
  I[n + 1:n, 2] <- 1

  ## different ways for setting up ids
  idex <- rep(1:2, each = n)
  idx <- as.numeric(c(id, rep(NA, n)))
  idy <- as.numeric(c(rep(NA, n), as.numeric(id) + nid))
  idxy <- as.numeric(c(id, as.numeric(id) + nid))

  data71 <- list(y = y, I = I,
                 idxy = idxy,
                 idex = idex,
                 idx = idx, idy = idy)

  ## independent random effects
  sim.joint0 <- y ~  -1 + I +
    f(idx, model = "iid") +
    f(idy, model = "iid")

  ## unstructured jmm

  sim.joint1 <- y ~  -1 + I +

    f(idxy, model = "iid2d", n = 2 * n,
      hyper = list(theta1 = list(param = c(4, 0.001, 0.001, 0))))

  ## pairwised jmm with fixed scale

  sim.joint2 <- y ~  -1 + I +

    f(idx, model = "iid2d", n = 2 * n,
      hyper = list(theta1 = list(param = c(4, 0.001, 0.001, 0)))) +

    f(idy, copy = "idx", fixed = TRUE)

  ## pairwised jmm with new beta scale to the second outcome
  sim.joint3 <- y ~  -1 + I +

    f(idx, model = "iid2d", n = 2 * n,
      hyper = list(theta1 = list(param = c(4, 0.001, 0.001, 0)))) +
    f(idy, copy = "idx", fixed = FALSE)

  inla.joint0 <- try(inla(sim.joint0,

                     family = c("gaussian", "gaussian"),

                     # control.family = list(initial = 10),

                     # control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
                     # control.compute = list(dic = TRUE),
                     data = data71))
  inla.joint1 <- try(inla(sim.joint1,
                     family = c("gaussian", "gaussian"),
                     # control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
                     # control.compute = list(dic = TRUE),
                     data = data71))

  inla.joint2 <- try(inla(sim.joint2,

                     family = c("gaussian", "gaussian"),

                     # control.family = list(initial = 10),

                     # control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
                     # control.compute = list(dic = TRUE),
                     data = data71))

  inla.joint3 <- try(inla(sim.joint3,

                     family = c("gaussian", "gaussian"),

                     # control.family = list(initial = 10),

                     # control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
                     # control.compute = list(dic = TRUE),
                     data = data71))

  cat(paste0("number ", seed, " iteration is done \n"))

  return(list(inla_1 = inla.joint1,
              inla_2 = inla.joint2,
              inla_0 = inla.joint0,
              inla_3 = inla.joint3,
              true_cov = Sigma,
              error_cov = cov(cbind(errorX, errorY)),
              sample_cov = cov(randomXY),
              sample_cor = cor(randomXY)))
}

Randy
```

messages.subject: Interpretation of the effective number of parameters
messages.subject_clean: Interpretation of the effective number of parameters
messages.body_plain:
I am fitting a simple GLMM with one continuous (Year) variate and a five level factor.  I am fitting a model with the following formula:

Response = alpha0_i _ alpha1_i . Year + alpha2_i . Year:habitat

My expectation was to fit an intercept, a difference in the intercept for the habitat class 2 to 5 and a Year slope for the first level of the habitat and four estimates of the differences in the slope for habitat 2 to 5.

A total of ten parameters.  The number of p.eff that is reported is around 44.  The table of fixed parameters shows the number of estimates as I expeced.

As with any model I fit I am sceptical but can anyone suggest what I should be reading to enlighten me as to the interpretation of the estimated number of effective parameters?

Nick.

messages.body_plain:
both DIC and WAIC has its own def of p.eff, and add to this, there are
various estimates of these,

like

> r=inla(y ~ 1, data=data.frame(y=1:10), control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,
waic=TRUE))
> r$waic$p.eff
[1] 1.675467946
> r$dic$p.eff
[1] 1.964058407
>

see attached.

I think the WAIC one is more reasonable (and the estimate used in INLA
is the variance of the score; see the attached paper).

what is Eff.Num.Parameters?   well, its 'what you define it to be'. its
more a 'concept/idea', as there is no objective definition in general
(maybe in the Gaussian case only).  its like two Normal random variables
with correlation rho.  if rho=0 we have two independent ones (like
p.eff=2), and iff |rho|=1 we have two perferct dependent ones (like
p.eff=1), and inbetween we have something between 1 and 2.

messages.body_plain:
You have been using fmesher indirectly via the devel version of
inlabru, and the upcoming INLA build will also use fmesher directly.

There's some more info here that will apply to the new INLA version
https://inlabru-org.github.io/fmesher/articles/inla_conversion.html

It's designed to work the same as the old functions for now, but allow
new features to be added.

The crs related code has been in inlabru for a while, including the
current CRAN version, but the functions were already called fm_* in
anticipation of being moved to the new package.

I can't really see what's wrong with your code; I'd need to run it on
my own system to step through to the error; if you're able to share
the data and code needed to trigger the error that would be great (by
private email).
But I suspect that a useful fix for you would be to convert the whole
thing to sf objects instead of sp.  Only some minor changes needed
apart from a bunch of sf::st_as_sf() on all your data objects (and
convert any SpatialPixels/Grid variables to terra::rast() instead).
Instead of comp(coordinates, ...) and domain=list(coordinates = mesh),
you'll need comp(geometry, ...) and domain=list(geometry = mesh).

Several of the inlabru website Articles have been updated to use sf
instead of sp, so have a look around the github.io <http://github.io> website for
inlabru.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

Thanks for this, I've convert my data and covariates as suggested.

Tried running the below code but giving me an error:

#### SPDE Only Model ####
# Specify hazard-rate detection function
hn <- function(distance, lsig) {1 - exp(-(distance / (exp(lsig)))^-1)}

# Define a (Matern) covariance function for the SPDE
matern <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(spatial_list$mesh,
                              prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01),
                              prior.range = c(10, 0.9))

# Specify components of model
cmp <- ~ mySPDE(main = geometry, model = matern) + lsig(1) + Intercept(1)

# Specify formula
form <- coordinates + distance ~ mySPDE +
  log(hn(distance, lsig)) +
  Intercept + log(2)

# Fit model with only SPDE
fit <- lgcp(
  components = cmp,
  data = spatial_list$nests,
  samplers = spatial_list$transects,
  domain = list(
    geometry = spatial_list$mesh,

    distance = INLA::inla.mesh.1d(seq(0, W, length.out = 30))
  ),

  formula = form,

  options = list(bru_initial = list(lsig = 2),

                 bru_verbose=4)
)

Error in fm_int.list(domain = domain, samplers = samplers, int.args = options[["bru_int_args"]]) :
  `sp` input detected but no `coordinates` domain present.

Do I need to amend coordinates in "form" too?

messages.subject: INLA version 23.08.18
messages.subject_clean: INLA version 23.08.18
messages.body_plain:
We're out with a new testing version for R-4.3, hopefully with a better
optimiser for hard models (read flat posteriors), but more importantly
that the 'fmesher' program is now in a separate R-package, 'fmesher'.
This program generate meshes for the spde-models. Here is info in the
NEWS

   Depend on the new fmesher package. By default, the new methods are
   used silently instead of the old fmesher standalone binary, and are
   meant to produce the same meshes etc as before. During a transition
   period, one can switch between the two code bases, as well as turn on
   informative deprecation warnings that point to which fmesher R
   function replaces the existing ones. See
   https://inlabru-org.github.io/fmesher/articles/inla_conversion.html
   for more details.

The fmesher-package is now on CRAN, but for some arch's might be a
little slow, so if you run into problems with the upgrade (not being
able to install/compile 'fmesher'), then try manually

options(repos=c(
            inlabruorg = "https://inlabru-org.r-universe.dev",
            INLA = "https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/testing",
            CRAN = "https://cran.rstudio.com"))
install.packages("fmesher")

and the upgrade R-INLA.

Let us know if there are any issues.

--
Håvard Rue
hr...@r-inla.org

Hello,

Hopefully its okay to post here about this, we are organizing a hackathon November 2-3 in Oslo for our package 4d-Modeller. This package is built on top of INLA and inlabru and is designed to make using the package easier for a wider audience. This includes shiny apps for building finite element meshes, an equation builder, and a map making tool for visualizing data. We would very much enjoy having participants join who have INLA/inlabru experience. There will be some amount of money for travel reimbursements for people coming from outside of Oslo.

Check out the preliminary schedule and more background on our website (https://4dmodeller.github.io/4DM_Hackathon/). And of course, sign up as soon as possible https://4dmodeller.github.io/4DM_Hackathon/_pages/register.html

Best,
--
John M. Aiken, PhD
Consultant, Expert Analytics
Researcher, The Njord Centre, University of Oslo
mnky9800n.github.io <http://mnky9800n.github.io>

messages.subject: Selection for inla.posterior.sample()
messages.subject_clean: Selection for inla.posterior.sample()
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am looking to draw posterior samples from an inla model, specifically for the prediction. I was using this line of code:

Post.Res <- inla.posterior.sample(100, res)

However, I realised this defaults to sampling from the whole model rather than the prediction stack. I gather you can use selection = list() to only sample from a section of the model but I'm not sure how to specify this? The model set up is below - if anyone could advise I would be very grateful.

# inla model for iteration 1 (data = it)
coo <- cbind(it$xcoo, it$ycoo)
mesh <- INLA::inla.mesh.2d(loc=coo, max.edge = c(2, 4), cutoff = 1)
spde.a <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh, alpha=2, constr = T)
indexs <- inla.spde.make.index("s", spde.a$n.spde)
A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = coo)
coop <- cbind(pred$xcoo, pred$ycoo)
Ap <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = coop)
stke <- inla.stack(tag="est", data=list(mos = it$mos),A = list(1, A), effects = list(data.frame(hab = it$hab, time=it$time), s = indexs)) # n=1080

messages.body_plain:
There is no speed-gain in using 'selection' as the whole model is
sampled, and then just the selction is stored.

If you need pointwise predictions only, you do not need simulations, but
can just compute them directly.

btw, the 'eval' functon has a vignette as its pretty useful and can be a
little confusing

H

Finn

Is there anyway inla parametrized in different way?

Is it possible that iid2d fitting a linear regression within each random effect?

Randy

On Wednesday, August 16, 2023 at 3:42:15 PM UTC-6 Helpdesk (Haavard Rue) wrote:

>
>
> This model should be straight forward, and its weird you do not get the
> correlation and sigma_{b2} correct. There is no confounding going on,
> right, like with with noise variances? You still get it wrong if you
> fix the likelihoods to be Gaussians with known precisions?
>
> I guess you do simulations so you can chose i=1..I, and j=1..J, and its
> still bad even with large I and J ?
>
> The 'iid2d' model use directly the (transformed) correlation as the
> hyperparameter, hence you should get it directly out in the results.
>
> Can you retry the same model without all covariates, ie just the iid2d
> model? This is also one of the examples in inla.doc('iid2d')
>
> There is a recent implementation, 'iidkd' that scales better for higher
> 'k', which uses a different parameterisation, but this should not change
> anything for dimension 2.
>
> Best
> H
>
>
> On Wed, 2023-08-16 at 13:42 -0700, Randy Jin wrote:
> > Hi everyone,
> >
> > I came across with the question for the second-type model you guys
> > discussed.
> >
> > Now I have multiple likelihood (2 outcomes), as well as multiple level
> > (longitudinal data with just random intercepts),
> > I want to estimate the correlation between random intercepts from two
> > separated likelihoods.
> >
> > So I used "iid2d", but it seems it does not work for the way I want.
> > (BTW, it seems work if I have two correlated random slopes no random
> > intercept).
> >
> > $$
> > \begin{split}
> > & \begin{cases}
> > x_{ij} \ | \ b_{1i} = \beta_{X0} + \beta_{X1}  \times {gender}_{x_i} +
> > \beta_{X2} \times visit_{x_{ij}}  + \beta_{X_3} \times group_i +
> > b_{1i} + \epsilon_{x_{ij}}  \\
> > y_{ij} \ |  b_{2i} = \beta_{Y0} + \beta_{Y1}  \times {gender}_{yi} +
> > \beta_{Y2} \times visit_{y_{ij}} + \beta_{Y_3} \times group_i +
> >  b_{2i} +  \epsilon_{y_{ij}} \\
> > \end{cases} \\
> > & \begin{bmatrix}
> >   b_1\\b_2
> > \end{bmatrix} \sim
> > MVN
> > \begin{pmatrix}
> >   \begin{bmatrix}
> >     0\\0
> >   \end{bmatrix} ,
> >   \begin{pmatrix}
> >     \sigma_{b_1}^2 & \rho\sigma_{b_1}\sigma_{b_2}\\
> >     \rho\sigma_{b_1}\sigma_{b_2} & \sigma_{b_2}^2
> >   \end{pmatrix}
> > \end{pmatrix} \\
> > &\epsilon_{x_{ij}} \sim N(0, \sigma_{\epsilon_X}^2)\\
> > &\epsilon_{y_{ij}} \sim N(0, \sigma_{\epsilon_Y}^2)
> > \end{split}
> > $$
> >
> > WX20230816-142706.png
> >
> > I am doing a 100 dataset simulation. So far INLA works perfect for
> > fixed effects, $sigma_{b1}$, and error terms $\epsilons$,
> > however I do not understand what is going on with the correlation
> > $\rho$ and the $sigma_{b2}$.
> > I assume INLA does not parametrize the model as I expected.
> >
> > Most of the examples I saw are correlated random slope and random
> > intercept.
> > But I want to model two correlated random intercepts from two
> > likelihood.
> > Any idea?
> >
> > Thanks!
> >
> > Randy
> >
> > ----------------------------------------------------------------------
> > ---------------------------------
> >
> > Currently I am using "iid2d" either with scaled or no scaled random
> > intercept
> >
> > sim.joint1 <- y ~  -1 + I + gender + visit + group +
> >     f(idxy,
> >        model = "iid2d",
> >        n = 2 * n,
> >       hyper = list(theta1 = list(param = c(4, 0.001, 0.001, 0))))
> >
> > sim.joint2 <- y ~  -1 + I + gender + visit + group +
> >     f(idx,
> >        model = "iid2d",
> >        n = 2 * n,
> >       hyper = list(theta1 = list(param = c(4, 0.001, 0.001, 0)))) +
> >     f(idy, copy = "idx",
> >         fixed = FALSE)
> >
> >  inla.joint1 <- try(inla(sim.joint1,
> >                      family = c("gaussian", "gaussian"),
> >                      # control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
> >                      # control.compute = list(dic = TRUE),
> >                      data = data71))
> >
> > On Thursday, September 30, 2021 at 9:55:10 AM UTC-6 INLA help wrote:
> > > Hi,
> > >
> > > This is a different model than the first one. In the first you have
> > > correlated residuals, now you have correlated residuals (u_ij) and
> > > an additional one (e_ij). This may lead to identifiability issues.
> > >
> > > For the first model you asked, the 'iid3d' model in INLA may be
> > > considered and so all the three variances are already fitted by this
> > > latent model, thus with no likelihood variances needed.
> > >
> > > best regards,
> > > Elias
> > >
> > > On Thu, 30 Sept 2021 at 16:47, Georgy Gomon <ggomon...@gmail.com>
> > > wrote:
> > > > Dear Håvard and Eliask,
> > > >
> > > > Thank you very much for your answers!
> > > > If I understand correctly to model residual covariances one needs
> > > > to split the 3 correlated measurements on a single individual into
> > > > 3 likelihoods and use random effects to model the correlation
> > > > between these likelihoods.
> > > > The model would thus have the following form:
> > > > INLA_vraag_2.png

> > > > first picture.
> > > > Is this correct?
> > > >
> > > > Many thanks,
> > > > Georgy
> > > > Op donderdag 30 september 2021 om 12:52:48 UTC+2 schreef
> > > > eliask...@gmail.com:
> > > > > ### An example in INLA
> > > > > set.seed(2021)
> > > > >
> > > > > ### Total of N individuals
> > > > > N <- 100
> > > > > ### n=3 correlated measurements per individual
> > > > >
> > > > > n <- 3
> > > > > data <- data.frame(
> > > > >     id=rep(1:N, each=n), ### order by individuals!
> > > > >     x=runif(N*n))
> > > > >
> > > > > Sigma <- matrix(c(5,-2,1, -2,3,1, 1,1,2), 3)
> > > > > Sigma
> > > > > cov2cor(Sigma)
> > > > > solve(Sigma)
> > > > >
> > > > > ### sampling a covariate setting up data such that the 3
> > > > > measurements on 1 individual are correlated
> > > > > errors <- matrix(rnorm(N*n), N) %*% chol(Sigma)
> > > > > cov(errors)
> > > > > cor(errors)
> > > > >
> > > > > data$y <- 3 + 2*data$x + as.vector(t(errors))
> > > > >
> > > > > library(INLA)
> > > > >
> > > > > data$i <- as.integer(t(matrix(1:(N*n), N))) ### inla order

> > > > >             data=data,
> > > > >             control.family = list(
> > > > >                 hyper = list(
> > > > >                     prec = list(initial = 15, fixed = TRUE))))
> > > > > res$summary.fix
> > > > > res$summary.hy
> > > > >
> > > > > cbind('TRUE'=c(diag(Sigma), cov2cor(Sigma)[lower.tri(Sigma)]),

> > > > > (1:n)]))
> > > > >
> > > > > On Thu, 30 Sept 2021 at 10:59, Helpdesk <he...@r-inla.org>
> > > > > wrote:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > INLA only support conditional independent data, but for
> > > > > > Gaussian
> > > > > > response, you can always just expand the latent field (or
> > > > > > linear
> > > > > > predictor) to have define dependent data. sometimes this
> > > > > > involve setting
> > > > > > the likelihood to have fixed high precision, like having AR1
> > > > > > depenendency in the observations.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > in these cases, you'll end up with a 'fake' linear predictor,
> > > > > > for which
> > > > > > a subset of it, is the real one.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > there are also generic iid models in dimension up to 10, with
> > > > > > general
> > > > > > covariance structure, that can be used for this (see

> > > > > >
> > > > > > Best
> > > > > > H

> > > > > > > Is it correct that INLA does not have the option to model
> > > > > > > correlation
> > > > > > > between Gaussian residuals?
> > > > > > > Instead of using random effects to model the correlation
> > > > > > > between
> > > > > > > measurements I would like to model the correlation between
> > > > > > > measurements
> > > > > > > using residuals.

> > > > > > > library(nlme)

> > > > > > > #Creating response

> > > > > > > fm1 <- gls(y ~ 1 + x, data=data,

messages.body_plain:
No,
this is unrelated to fmesher and is instead due to "readlink -f" (as
is used in the mac.arm64/inla.run script) not being valid on pre-12.3
mac.
Finn

messages.body_plain:
the issue is option '-f' in command 'readlink' which was introduced at
an MacOS upgrade, maybe 13.0  but I have not checked.  I know it was not
there for earlier versions as we have a shell-function mimicing this
behaviour as the 'follow links until the end' was not available

the solution is to upgrade the MacOS

messages.body_snippet:
the issue is option '-f' in command 'readlink' which was introduced at
an MacOS upgrade, maybe 13.0  but I have not checked.  I know it was not
there for earlier versions as we have a shell-function m

It was introduced in 12.3 according to the blog post.
Finn

You can set yourself to a "reasonable" small fraction. However, if you
set it too small you may encounter numerical problems.

messages.subject: Empirical Bayes for geostatistical models
messages.subject_clean: Empirical Bayes for geostatistical models
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
Do you have some insight on how much we lose in terms of prediction and estimation when using an Empirical Bayes approach instead of full INLA/MCMC/whatever in a geostatistical model ?
I think the answer to be "yes" with data sets that give some significant freedom to the posterior distribution for the SPDE/covariance parameters. Håvard <https://groups.google.com/g/r-inla-discussion-group/c/ShL-SzV0Ryg> and L Held's disease mapping papers identified and addressed the issue of the coupling of the latent field and the high-level parameters. Do you confirm this lead ?
However, with large data sets that should give very slim posterior distributions, do you think that there is a need for full exploration in order to predict and estimate correctly the spatial effects and the effects of covariates ?
Thanks in advance
Sébastien

messages.body_plain:
>From the philosifical point of view, 'empirical bayes' is pretty bad or
maybe close to as bad as it can get, as the 'implicite prior' is a point
mass at the mode and all uncertainty are ignored. Variational Bayes is
not even defined for this...

its is very handy if your model contains critical parameters which are
influencial for the model, like the tail-index/parameter for extremes.
including the uncertainty can make a huge impact for predictions, so if
you ignore it, it will be an easier sell... well, that was a joke, but I
think this is the way many sees it, without saying it clearly.

the additional cost of not doing 'eb' is quite moderate, so there is
less to gain computationally these days

if the uncertaintay is small, there is little difference, which can
justufy using 'eb' but there are no formal justifcation in general

H

messages.body_plain:
The first report about this error message on the list I could find was
  https://groups.google.com/g/r-inla-discussion-group/c/O-Vn_LFJkqw/m/nTJ86HErBAAJ
and wasn't traced to a specific function or package, but the root
cause was clear; a version of some package, likely Matrix, since
fixupDN() is an unexported function in that package, was installed on
a pre-4.2 version of R, but the ...length() and ...names() features
weren't introduced to R in previous versions, such as 4.1, and the
previous reports of this issue were resolved by upgrading R to a 4.2.x
version.

If you rerun with inla(..., safe = FALSE) you should be able to
produce traceback() output. From that, we may be able to pinpoint the
source of the problem.

Finn
